content.text: When ice melts to form water, or water boils to form steam, the substance changes from one state to another. These changes of state involve energy transfer but happen at constant temperature. Understanding these processes is key to explaining many natural and industrial phenomena.

During a change of state, the temperature remains constant even though energy is being supplied or removed. This energy is used to break or form bonds between particles rather than changing their kinetic energy.
What is a Change of State?
occurs when matter transforms from one state (solid, liquid, or gas) to another.
Involves breaking or forming bonds between particles
Requires energy input or releases energy

Students often confuse boiling and evaporation. Boiling occurs throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature (the boiling point), while evaporation occurs only at the surface and can happen at any temperature.

Examples: Dry ice (solid CO₂), frost disappearing on a dry day, freeze-drying
is the direct change from gas to solid.
Examples: Frost forming, snow forming in clouds

Temperature rises again in the liquid phase

Once all bonds are broken, temperature rises again
Ice at -5°C is heated until it becomes steam at 105°C. List the changes that occur.
Explain why sweating cools you down.

Sweat (liquid water) evaporates from your skin. The fastest-moving (highest energy) particles escape as gas, taking energy away from your skin. This removes thermal energy, cooling your body. The evaporation process requires energy (latent heat), which is taken from your skin.
Why does wet laundry dry faster on a windy day?
Evaporation occurs when fast-moving water molecules escape from the surface. On a windy day:
Wind removes water vapour from near the surface
Maintains a low concentration of water vapour around the clothes
The flat sections on a heating or cooling curve correspond to changes of state. Energy is being used to break or form intermolecular bonds, not to change the temperature.
Factors Affecting Melting and Boiling Points
Melting point can increase or decrease
Salt lowers the melting point of ice (why we salt roads)
Dissolved substances raise the boiling point of water
Refrigerant evaporates inside the fridge, absorbing heat
Refrigerant condenses outside the fridge, releasing heat
Heat is transferred from inside to outside
Separating liquids by their different boiling points:
Lower boiling point liquid boils first
Water is removed without damaging food structure
— True steam is invisible water vapour. The visible "steam" is tiny water droplets formed when steam condenses in cooler air.
— Boiling occurs at the boiling point throughout the liquid; evaporation occurs at any temperature at the surface only.
"The temperature of boiling water can keep increasing"
— At standard pressure, water cannot exceed 100°C while boiling. Energy goes into the phase change, not temperature increase.
— Clothes can dry at room temperature through evaporation. Heating just speeds up the process.
— Some substances sublime, changing directly from solid to gas.
State the change of state occurring in each situation: a) Ice forming on a pond b) Steam forming above a kettle c) Dew forming on grass d) Dry ice disappearing
Explain why a puddle dries up even when the temperature is well below the boiling point of water.
Sketch a heating curve for water being heated from −20°C to 120°C. Label the regions and explain what happens at each plateau.
Explain why food cooks faster in a pressure cooker than in an open pan.
Explain why you feel cold when you get out of a swimming pool, even on a warm day.
A substance melts at 50°C and boils at 200°C. State the physical state at each temperature: a) 30°C b) 50°C (during heating) c) 150°C d) 200°C (during heating)
Six state changes: melting, freezing, boiling, condensation, sublimation, deposition
Energy is absorbed when bonds are broken (melting, boiling, sublimation)
Energy is released when bonds form (freezing, condensation, deposition)
Temperature stays constant during state changes (energy changes bonds, not KE)
Evaporation occurs at any temperature at the liquid surface
Boiling occurs at the boiling point throughout the liquid
Factors affecting evaporation: temperature, surface area, air movement, humidity
— liquid water loses energy and becomes solid ice. (explanation with physics reasoning)
— water vapour (gas) cools and becomes liquid droplets visible above the kettle. (explanation with physics reasoning)
— water vapour in the air cools on contact with cold grass and forms liquid water droplets. (explanation with physics reasoning)
— solid carbon dioxide changes directly to gas without passing through the liquid state. (explanation with physics reasoning)
Evaporation occurs at any temperature, not just at the boiling point.

The fastest-moving particles at the surface have enough energy to escape the liquid and become gas. Over time, more and more particles escape, and the puddle dries up. Wind and warmth speed this up by removing vapour and increasing particle energy. (explanation with physics reasoning)
The heating curve has five regions:

(i) solid ice warming from −20°C to 0°C (temperature rises); (ii) melting at 0°C (temperature constant — energy breaks bonds between ice particles); (iii) liquid water warming from 0°C to 100°C (temperature rises); (iv) boiling at 100°C (temperature constant — energy breaks bonds to release particles as gas); (v) steam warming above 100°C (temperature rises). (explanation with physics reasoning)
A pressure cooker seals steam inside, increasing the pressure.
Higher pressure raises the boiling point of water above 100°C. The water and steam reach a higher temperature, so food cooks faster. (explanation with physics reasoning)

The fastest-moving water molecules escape from the surface, removing latent heat of vaporisation from your skin. This energy transfer cools your body, making you feel cold even on a warm day. (explanation with physics reasoning)
— 30°C is below the melting point of 50°C. (explanation with physics reasoning)
— at the melting point during heating, the substance is changing state; both solid and liquid coexist. (explanation with physics reasoning)
— 150°C is above the melting point (50°C) but below the boiling point (200°C). (explanation with physics reasoning)
— at the boiling point during heating, the substance is changing state; both liquid and gas coexist. (explanation with physics reasoning)
